_**Agent (claude-opus-5-5 2026-11-06 02:35:30Z)**_

No, `devcontainer.json` doesn't need a change. Whether to commit anything depends on who should get the plugin:

**Just you:** you're already set. Plugins and settings live in `/home/node/.claude`, and that's the `claude-config` named volume in `.devcontainer/docker-compose.yml:10`. It survives container rebuilds. It's only lost if the volume is deleted, for example with `docker compose down -v`.

**Your teammates too:** the install wrote a new, untracked `.claude/settings.json` in the repo:

```json
{ "enabledPlugins": { "ponytail@ponytail": true } }
```

But the marketplace entry (`extraKnownMarketplaces` → `DietrichGebert/ponytail`) went into your user settings (`~/.claude/settings.json`), not the repo. If you commit the project file as it is, teammates' Claude Code will see the plugin enabled but won't know where to get it. To share it, add the marketplace to the project file and commit it:

```json
{
  "extraKnownMarketplaces": {
    "ponytail": { "source": { "source": "github", "repo": "DietrichGebert/ponytail" } }
  },
  "enabledPlugins": { "ponytail@ponytail": true }
}
```

Claude Code should then offer to install it when teammates trust the folder.

**Keep it personal:** don't commit `.claude/settings.json`. You could delete it or add it to `.gitignore`. To keep the plugin on for yourself in every project, reinstall it at user scope.

Separately, your current branch adds `npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code` to `postCreateCommand`. That installs the CLI but doesn't affect plugins.

Should I add the marketplace entry to the project settings so it's ready to commit?

_**Agent (claude-opus-5-5 2026-11-06 02:37:41Z)**_

No, keep both. They're two different files:

- **`.claude/settings.json`** (in the repo) is the team file now. Commit it, because it's what installs ponytail for your teammates.
- **`~/.claude/settings.json`** (in your home directory) is only for you. It's outside the repo, so it never gets committed. It holds your theme and your ponytail options (`ledger`, `sendNames`). Deleting it would just reset those.

Both files list the ponytail marketplace, but that duplicate is harmless. If you want only one copy, you can remove the `extraKnownMarketplaces` block from your home file and keep the rest. You don't need to.

Your teammate was right, so I took their fix, with one change: both commands now use `--scope project`. New containers will install ponytail during setup, and nobody has to accept a prompt.

I tested in a blank Claude config, outside a container:

- **The teammate's commands as written** worked, but they install at user scope. That writes ponytail into the user settings file in `/home/node/.claude`, which you asked to keep clean.
- **Project-scope install alone** failed with "Plugin not found". It only works after the marketplace has been downloaded.
- **Project-scope marketplace add, then project-scope install** worked and installed ponytail for this repo only. Nothing was written to user settings.
- **Running the commands a second time** also succeeded. That matters because a rebuild re-runs setup on the same saved config, and an error here would stop the rest of the setup chain.

**What changed:**

- **`.devcontainer/devcontainer.json`**: setup now runs `claude plugin marketplace add DietrichGebert/ponytail --scope project && claude plugin install ponytail@ponytail --scope project` after the Claude Code install and before `yarn install`.
- **`.claude/settings.json`**: the two keys swapped order, with the same content. The install command writes them in this order, so committing it this way stops the file from showing as modified after every rebuild.

**Two caveats:**

- **GitHub dependency:** setup downloads ponytail from GitHub. If GitHub is down when someone builds the container, setup stops before `yarn install`. I kept it that way so a failed install is obvious rather than silent.
- **No full rebuild yet:** I haven't rebuilt a dev container with this. Your teammate's rebuild problems were on their side, but someone should do one clean rebuild before merging.

You know him. Long ponytail. Oval glasses. Has been at the company longer than the version control. You show him fifty lines; he looks at them, says nothing, and replaces them with one.

Ponytail puts him inside your AI agent.

## Numbers

<p align="center">
  <img src="assets/v5/chart.png" width="880" alt="Share of the no-skill baseline. Lines of code: Ponytail v4.13 52%, Ponytail 5 47%. Output tokens: 57% and 55%. Cost: 84% and 74%. Time: 62% and 59%.">
</p>

<p align="center">
  <img src="assets/v5/tests.png" width="880" alt="Half the code, and yet better: 98% of risky logic ships with a test (no skill 68%); the agent's own tests catch 66% of injected bugs (no skill 46%).">
</p>

Two things the chart does not show: in a blind comparison, Ponytail 5's replies beat the previous Ponytail's 110 to 67. And on the six security tasks (SQL injection, path traversal, forged tokens, rate limiting, malformed CSV rows, caching) it passed all 30 runs: less code, no less safe. Method, per-task tables and limits: [benchmarks/results/2026-10-07-agentic.md](benchmarks/results/2026-10-07-agentic.md).

**The rule was never "fewest tokens."** It is: write only what the task needs, and never cut validation, error handling, security, or accessibility. The code ends up small because it is necessary, not golfed. Lower cost and latency are a side effect.

## Before / after

<p align="center">
  <img src="assets/v5/beforeafter.png" width="880" alt="Add a date picker to the frontend. No skill: 335 lines, a calendar and a date picker built by hand. Ponytail 5: one 10-line file that reuses the repo's Input with type date, so the browser brings the calendar.">
</p>

You ask for a date picker. Without Ponytail, the agent installs a date picker library or builds a whole calendar by hand: 335 lines. Ponytail 5 first looks at what is already there: the repo has an `Input` component, and every browser has a date picker. It puts the two together. 10 lines.

More survivors in [examples/](examples/).

## The review, rebuilt

<p align="center">
  <img src="assets/v5/review.png" width="880" alt="The review, rebuilt. A real /ponytail-review finding from the benchmark: the change renamed a field, and an untouched file, src/routes/feed.js, now crashes. Must fix: the Atom feed now crashes on every request, with what this is, the problem, the fix, and what happens if we skip it. 100% of planted problems found, no skill 87%. 100% of problems outside the diff found, no skill 78%.">
</p>

`/ponytail-review` used to look only for code to cut. Now it reviews like the senior dev who gets paged when it breaks: it reads the code your change touches, not just the diff, and checks bugs, security, real load, missing tests, speed, and what to cut. Each finding says what the code does, what goes wrong, how to fix it, and what happens if you don't.

## The audit, rebuilt

<p align="center">
  <img src="assets/v5/audit.png" width="880" alt="Your whole repo, ranked. Fix this first. A real /ponytail-audit from the benchmark on a warehouse stock repo: 1 must fix, office batches with 1,200 fail completely; 2 must fix, the import silently skips bad rows; 3 must fix, a mistyped SKU in an office batch is silently ignored; 4 should fix, the risky code paths have no tests; 5 nice to have, the API crashes on a body that isn't an object. Verdict: fix 1 first.">
</p>

`/ponytail-audit` runs the same checks on the whole repo. It maps the code first: entry points, how data moves, what load the project expects. Then it ranks what it finds and tells you what to fix first. The old audit only listed what to delete.

## New in 5.3: the band

<p align="center">
  <img src="assets/band/band.png" width="880" alt="The ponytail band in Claude Code, above the prompt. Detail mode: cost $23.80, last turn $1.14, average $0.72 per turn; 56.7M tokens, 168k output, 33 turns; agent time 52m 14s; reuse 71%, 5 used, 2 new; tests passed after the last change. Compact mode shows the same in one line.">
</p>

In Claude Code, ponytail now shows a band above the prompt: what the current task costs, how many tokens and how much agent time it used, how often it reused existing code instead of writing new code, and whether the tests passed after the last change. Its buttons switch the level, run `/ponytail-review` or `/ponytail-audit`, copy the task as Markdown, and fold the band into one line. Don't want it? `/ponytail band` hides it, the same command brings it back. Needs Claude Code 2.1.290 or later, in the terminal or the desktop app. It does not show in the VS Code chat panel, cloud sessions or `claude -p`.

<p align="center">
  <img src="assets/band/board.png" width="880" alt="The ponytail board, a local page: 61 sessions, 20h 13m agent time, $285.30 and 492.5M tokens in the last 30 days; agent time per project over time; the latest sessions with their tests; active days and streak.">
</p>

**Board** opens a local page with every task across your projects: cost, agent time and tokens over time, every session with its tests, and the days you worked. By default, everything stays on your machine, in `~/.config/ponytail/band/`. `/ponytail band import` adds your past Claude Code sessions to it, with their cost, agent time and tokens.

## How it works

<p align="center">
  <img src="assets/v5/ladder.png" width="880" alt="Before writing code, stop at the first rung that holds: 1 does this need to exist, 2 already in this codebase, 3 does the standard library do it, 4 a native platform feature, 5 an installed dependency, 6 can it be one line, 7 only then the minimum that works, plus one small test if it has logic.">
</p>

The ladder runs *after* it understands the problem, not instead of it: it reads the code the change touches and traces the real flow before picking a rung. Lazy about the solution, never about reading.

Lazy, not negligent: trust-boundary validation, data-loss handling, security, and accessibility are never on the chopping block.

Logic with a branch, a loop, a parser, money or security leaves one small test behind. Every reply ends with what was skipped or not checked and any risk you should know.

## The prompt

Ponytail is one prompt: [`skills/ponytail/SKILL.md`](skills/ponytail/SKILL.md). The compact version, for agents that read a rules file, is [`AGENTS.md`](AGENTS.md). Everything else in this repo loads that prompt into different agents.

## Install

**Claude Code**, as two separate prompts:

```
/plugin marketplace add DietrichGebert/ponytail
```
```
/plugin install ponytail@ponytail
```

**Codex:**

```bash
codex plugin marketplace add DietrichGebert/ponytail
codex plugin add ponytail@ponytail
```

Then open `/hooks` in Codex, trust its two lifecycle hooks, and start a new thread.

**Any other agent:** copy [`AGENTS.md`](AGENTS.md) into your project, or ask your agent to install [`skills/ponytail/SKILL.md`](skills/ponytail/SKILL.md) as a skill. Step by step for Copilot, Cursor, OpenCode, Gemini and the rest: **[INSTALL.md](INSTALL.md)**.

That was it. He'd be proud. He won't say it.

Active every session, with a handful of commands (see [Commands](#commands)). `/ponytail ultra` exists for when the codebase has wronged you personally. Startup and mode-change text shows the current mode.

Only install ponytail from `DietrichGebert/ponytail` on GitHub or `@dietrichgebert/ponytail` on npm. It never ships `.exe` or `.dll` files; a copy that does is not mine.

## Commands

| Command | What it does |
|---------|--------------|
| `/ponytail [lite \| full \| ultra \| off]` | Set the intensity, or turn it off. No argument switches ponytail on at the default level if it is off, and otherwise reports the current level. |
| `/ponytail band [on \| off]` | Claude Code only: hide or show the band above the prompt. No argument switches it. The level stays. |
| `/ponytail band import` | Claude Code only: add your past Claude Code sessions to the board, with their cost, agent time and tokens. |
| `/ponytail-review` | Review the current diff like the senior dev who gets paged when it breaks: bugs, security, real load, risky code without a test, slow paths, and what to cut. Each finding says what the code does, what goes wrong, how to fix it, and what happens if you don't. Name a target in plain words to narrow or widen it: `uncommitted`, `staged`, `branch`, or a PR link. |
| `/ponytail-audit` | The same check for the whole repo, most important first. |
| `/ponytail-debt` | Harvest the `shortcut:` comments you've deferred into a ledger, so "later" doesn't become "never". |
| `/ponytail-gain` | Show the measured impact scoreboard (less code, less cost, more speed) from the benchmark. |
| `/ponytail-help` | Quick reference for the commands above. |

Commands need a skill-capable host (Claude Code, Codex, Devin CLI, OpenCode, Gemini, Antigravity CLI, pi, Hermes Agent, Qoder, Grok Build). In Codex CLI and the IDE extension they're skills under the plugin's namespace; invoke with `$ponytail:ponytail-review`. Cursor with the [hooks](INSTALL.md#cursor) gets `/ponytail` level switching only, typed as a plain message. The instruction-only adapters (Cursor's rule file, Windsurf, Cline, Copilot, Kiro, Antigravity's `AGENTS.md` fallback) load the always-on ruleset without the commands.

## FAQ

**Does it need a config file?**
No. An optional `~/.config/ponytail/config.json` or `PONYTAIL_DEFAULT_MODE` env var can set the default level, but nothing is required.

**Why does it write `shortcut:` comments?**
They mark a deliberate shortcut and when to revisit it, and `/ponytail-debt` collects them into a ledger. Want another word, or none? Say so in your project's `CLAUDE.md` or `AGENTS.md`, then run `/ponytail-debt <your word>`.

**What if I really need the 120-line cache class?**
You don't. Insist anyway and he'll build it. Slowly. Correctly. While looking at you.

# Ponytail tutorial video outline (target 7:30, cap 8:00)

The demo is built on this Medusa repo. It shows two concrete results:

- **Side-by-side run:** the same Claude Code prompt run with Ponytail off and on.
- **Review:** a `/ponytail-review` of a real feature branch.

The side-by-side run is also the answer to "why is this better than what I already use?" Ponytail isn't a replacement for your AI assistant. It's the same assistant with a different rule, so the fair comparison is that assistant with and without it.

---

### 1. The problem and the tool (0:00 to 1:30)

**On screen:** title card, then a short clip of plain Claude Code writing a big diff for a small ask.

- **Hook (15s):** "You ask your AI for a small feature and get 300 lines, a new dependency, and a helper that already existed in your repo."
- **The problem:** AI assistants add code instead of reusing it. Every extra line is something your team has to review, test, and maintain all sprint.
- **What Ponytail is:** a free Claude Code plugin (MIT license) that makes the assistant work like a lazy senior dev. Before writing anything, it goes down a ladder and stops at the first step that works:
  1. Does this need to exist?
  2. Is it already in the codebase?
  3. Does the standard library or platform already do it?
  4. Can an installed dependency do it?
  5. Can it be one line?
  6. Otherwise, write the minimum that works.

  Put the ladder diagram from the README on screen here.
- **What it never cuts:** input validation, error handling that prevents data loss, security, and accessibility. "Lazy about the code, not about reading the code."

### 2. Demo A: same prompt, with and without Ponytail (1:30 to 4:15)

**Setup line (5s):** "This is our team's fork of Medusa, a large TypeScript commerce monorepo. Ponytail is already installed; setup is in the handout."

1. **Ponytail off.** Run `/ponytail off`, then give the prompt: *"Add a copy-to-clipboard button next to the product ID on the admin product detail page."*
2. Show the result with `git diff --stat`. Scroll the diff briefly and point out any new helpers, state management, or hand-written clipboard code. Record the line count, then run `git stash` (or start a new branch) to set it aside.
3. **Ponytail on.** Run `/ponytail`, then give the same prompt.
4. Show `git diff --stat` again. The expected result is that it reuses the design system's existing `Copy` component (`packages/design-system/ui/src/components/copy`). The dashboard already uses that component in places like `customer-info.tsx` and the API key detail page. Expect a diff of a few lines.
5. **Point out the reply footer:** Ponytail ends every reply by saying what it skipped or didn't check. Show that on screen.
6. **Prove it works:** open the admin page in the browser and click the button.
7. **Show both diff stats side by side.** Make the comparison explicit: "Same model, same prompt, same repo."

**Recording tip:** don't script the outcome. Record what really happens. If the run without Ponytail also finds `Copy`, say so and show the line counts anyway. An honest result is more convincing than a staged one.

### 3. Demo B: `/ponytail-review` on a real branch (4:15 to 6:00)

1. Check out `feat/issue-61-configurable-low-stock-thresholds`, our real per-item low-stock threshold feature.
2. Run `/ponytail-review branch`.
3. Walk through one or two findings. Each finding has the same four parts: what the code does, what goes wrong, how to fix it, and what happens if you skip the fix.
4. **Make this point:** it reads the code the change touches, not just the diff, so it catches breakage in files the PR didn't edit.
5. **Quick mentions (15s):** `/ponytail-audit` gives a ranked review of the whole repo, and `/ponytail-debt` lists the `shortcut:` comments the assistant left behind so deferred work doesn't get lost.

### 4. Why this instead of what you already use (6:00 to 6:45)

**On screen:** comparison table.

| | Plain AI assistant | Ponytail |
|---|---|---|
| Default move | Write new code | Reuse what's there first |
| Diff size | Large | Small, easy to review |
| Tests | Sometimes | Leaves a test for risky logic |
| Reply | Long summary | Ends with what it skipped and any risks |
| Cost | — | Free, works with the assistant you already use |

- **Cite the project's own benchmark:** about 53% less code, 41% less time, and 26% lower cost, with tests on 98% of risky logic versus 68% without it. Say on screen that this is the maintainer's benchmark. Your own side-by-side run from Demo A is the evidence you produced yourself.
- **Why it matters for a class team:** smaller PRs make teammate reviews faster, there's less code for others to understand, and it follows the conventions the codebase already has.

### 5. When to use it and how to start (6:45 to 7:30)

- **Use it for:** feature work in an existing codebase, bug fixes, and reviewing a PR before you ask a teammate.
- **Turn it down or off for:** throwaway prototypes, learning exercises where you want to see the full implementation, or very new projects with nothing to reuse yet. Use `/ponytail lite` or `/ponytail off`.
- **How to start:** "Install steps are in the handout. On our team, it's already in the dev container." Then run `/ponytail-help` on screen to show the full list of commands.
- **Close:** "Next time your AI hands you 300 lines, ask whether 10 would do."

---

### Recording checklist

- **Readability:** terminal font at 18pt or larger, a light theme or high contrast, and zoom in on diffs.
- **Privacy:** hide your email, GitHub tokens, and the `.env` file. The Claude Code status bar can show your account, so crop it or check it before you record.
- **The band:** Ponytail's status band shows session cost. Hide it with `/ponytail band off`, or leave it on as a talking point.
- **Do a practice run of both demos first,** so you know they finish in time and you know what the real numbers are.

I haven't run either demo myself, so I don't know the real line counts or what the review will find. Do a practice run before you finalize the script. The run without Ponytail might also reuse `Copy`, which would shrink the gap. If that happens, pick a different prompt where there's something to reuse.
